issues.legal_issue: Applying tenant-protection legislation to a ruler’s private lands does not violate a merger agreement guaranteeing full ownership, use, and enjoyment of those lands.
material_facts: The lands had been determined to be the ruler’s private property under the merger arrangements.
Legislation was extended to the merged territory to protect tenants, and applied to the private lands on the basis that the ruler remained their owner.
The legislation restricted ejectment and provided for fair rent and occupancy rights for tenants.
issues.conclusion: The legislation did not infringe the guarantee of full ownership, use, and enjoyment; the guarantee did not exempt the private lands from generally applicable tenant-protection restrictions.
issues.legal_principle: The merger guarantee protected the ruler’s title against a claim that the lands were State property; it did not guarantee immunity from legislation applicable to other owners. Any guarantee was co-extensive with the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property under Article 19(1)(f), subject to permissible restrictions under Article 19(5). The Court followed State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga, [1952] S.C.R. 889, and Visheshwar Rao v. The State of Madhya Pradesh, [1952] S.C.R. 1020.

predicates.appeal_from_quashing_tenant_proceedings: The case is an appeal from a decision quashing proceedings brought under tenant-protection law.
predicates.merger_guarantee_recognizes_private_titl: The merger arrangement recognizes the ruler’s title to the lands as private property rather than State property.
predicates.tenant_protection_law_applies_to_owner: Tenant-protection legislation applies restrictions to the owner for the protection of tenants occupying the lands.

issues.definition: When an appeal from quashed tenant proceedings concerns recognized private title subject to tenant-protection legislation, the private-property guarantee is not infringed merely because that legislation restricts the owner.

issues.legal_issue: A dispute between a landowner and tenants over the application of tenant-protection law to an eviction is not barred from court jurisdiction merely because the landowner’s title was recognized in a merger agreement.
material_facts: The dispute concerned the tenants’ eviction from private lands and their applications for restoration under tenant-protection law.
The lands were treated as the ruler’s private property, and the legislation proceeded on the basis that he owned them.
The dispute was between the tenants and the owner, rather than a dispute over whether the lands belonged to the State.
issues.conclusion: Article 363 did not bar the courts from entertaining the dispute.
issues.legal_principle: Article 363 excludes jurisdiction over disputes arising out of provisions of specified agreements with rulers. A landlord–tenant dispute arising from an owner’s eviction of tenants under legislation, where the owner’s title is not disputed, does not arise out of the merger agreement.

predicates.landlord_tenant_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute between a landowner and persons claiming to hold land as tenants.
predicates.eviction_under_tenant_protection_law: The tenants challenge their eviction and seek relief under tenant-protection law.
predicates.private_title_not_disputed: The dispute proceeds on the basis that the landowner owns the lands as private property, rather than contesting whether the lands are State property.

issues.definition: A landlord–tenant proceeding about eviction under tenant-protection law remains within court jurisdiction when the owner’s private title is not disputed.

issues.legal_issue: The merged-state law’s extended definitions determine who is a landlord and tenant for the application of tenant-protection law, even if the original Act’s definitions do not cover their relationship.
material_facts: The tenants held the lands under the owner.
The merged-state law defined a tenant as a person holding land under another who was, or but for a special contract would be, liable to pay rent to that person.
The merged-state law defined a landlord as the person immediately under whom the tenant held the land.
issues.conclusion: The tenants qualified as tenants and the owner qualified as their landlord under the merged-state law’s definitions.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(a) of the Orissa Merged States (Laws) Act, 1950, including its explanation, supplied the applicable definitions of “landlord” and “tenant.” Those definitions were sufficient even if the definitions in section 2(c) and section 2(g) of the Orissa Tenants Protection Act, 1948, would not independently cover the relationship.

predicates.tenant_protection_proceeding: The case concerns proceedings seeking relief under tenant-protection law.
predicates.tenant_holds_land_under_owner: The person claiming tenant status holds the land under the person claimed to be the landlord.
predicates.rent_liability_exists_or_is_displaced_by: The person holding the land is liable to pay rent to the person under whom the land is held, or would be liable but for a special contract.

issues.definition: In a tenant-protection proceeding, a person holding land under another with actual or contract-displaced rent liability is a tenant, and the person immediately under whom the land is held is the landlord.

issues.legal_issue: The tenant-protection Act and the merged-state law operate together, giving revenue courts jurisdiction over landlord–tenant proceedings in the merged territory.
material_facts: The merged-state law extended the tenant-protection Act to the merged territory.
The merged-state law directed that suits and proceedings between landlords and tenants be instituted and tried in revenue courts.
The owner argued that the merged-state law’s provisions displaced the Act’s court procedures and left a gap in jurisdiction.
The revenue officer had heard the tenants’ restoration applications under the Act.
issues.conclusion: Read together, the laws gave the revenue officer jurisdiction to hear the dispute, and the restoration orders were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Orissa Merged States (Laws) Act, 1950, extended the Orissa Tenants Protection Act, 1948, to the merged territory. Section 7 of the 1950 Act made supplementary modifications to tenancy law, including directing landlord–tenant proceedings to revenue courts. The two Acts must be read together, so the Act’s relevant procedures and the merged-state law’s modifications applied without a jurisdictional gap.

predicates.tenant_protection_proceeding_in_merged_t: The case concerns a tenant-protection proceeding in territory incorporated into an absorbing province.
predicates.tenant_protection_law_extended_to_territ: The tenant-protection law has been extended to the incorporated territory.
predicates.landlord_tenant_proceedings_assigned_to_: The applicable law directs landlord–tenant proceedings to revenue courts.

issues.definition: When tenant-protection proceedings arise in incorporated territory where the law applies and landlord–tenant proceedings are assigned to revenue courts, the revenue court has jurisdiction.
